column3: A brief lifting of punishment followed by return frames "a little" as temporary exposure, supporting the verse's short reprieve while retaining its warning.
It supplies the later destination of the mujrimun: they are driven to Hell, extending the addressee's penal horizon.
Its brief enjoyment explicitly gives way to compelled movement toward severe punishment, closely paralleling both halves of 77:46.
It recasts worldly duration as only little in retrospect, sharpening the temporal scale of the commanded enjoyment.
The preceding command to proceed toward what they denied establishes the judgment setting in which 77:46 speaks.
A favorable, time-bounded enjoyment follows repentance, providing a contrasting conditional enjoyment rather than the culpable one in 77:46.
Brief enjoyment and painful punishment form an explicit compact parallel to 77:46.
The closing challenge underscores the denial motif surrounding the address to the guilty, though it adds no food or duration detail.
Provision for humans and livestock presents enjoyment as granted sustenance, a benign counterpoint to the guilty persons' brief enjoyment.
The same eat-and-drink imperative is attached to what was done, supplying a rewarded counterpart to 77:46's accusatory imperative.
The command toward a three-branched shadow continues the punitive route after 77:46's declaration.
Eating, enjoyment, and distracting hope are joined before eventual knowledge, strongly clarifying the warning rather than approval in 77:46.
The exact eat-and-drink wording is positively qualified by prior deeds, making its contrast with 77:46 especially precise.
The repeated woe locates 77:46 within the refrain against deniers and reinforces its judicial tone.
It calls worldly enjoyment little against the better hereafter, supplying the same evaluative scale in a different situation.
Naming a people mujrimun supports the culpability term in 77:46, but contributes no enjoyment or brevity imagery.
Eating illicit gain offers a morally charged consumption parallel, though the verse concerns judgment and justice rather than a temporary reprieve.
It identifies worldly benefit as little when preferred over the hereafter, reinforcing 77:46's reduction of present enjoyment.
The same imperative is a deserved, pleasant share for prior good, a direct contrary reading to the guilty addressees of 77:46.
The alleged shade gives no shade or protection from flame, detailing the punishment scene that brackets 77:46.
Food restricted to the sinful makes consumption itself a mark of penal classification, a close secondary parallel.
Mujrimun are portrayed as agents of misguidance, expanding the moral content of the label without addressing temporary enjoyment.
The refrain immediately after 77:46 confirms that its address belongs to the woe against deniers.
Hidden and open arrogance remains known and accountable, offering a general basis for the culpability in 77:46.
Escape from death only yields brief enjoyment, another direct statement that postponement cannot secure a lasting outcome.
The command for mujrimun to separate supplies a judgment-day sorting parallel to 77:46's direct address to them.
Worldly life is a deceptive enjoyment that withers, explaining how real benefit can still mislead when mistaken for permanence.
The strangers are called unknown; it has no clear contribution to culpable, brief enjoyment.
The palace-sized sparks develop the fire toward which the guilty warning is oriented.
Mujrimun appear bound in chains on that day, making visible the consequence attached to their status in 77:46.
Brief enjoyment followed by Hell closely parallels the verse, despite addressing prosperity rather than its eat-and-enjoy imperative.
The repeated woe resumes the denial refrain after the judgment scenes, reinforcing the setting only.
Eating is linked to acknowledged divine naming and faith, offering a lawful, accountable contrast to unqualified guilty consumption.
Those who followed luxurious enjoyment are called mujrimun, tightly connecting culpability with indulgent attachment.
It warns that hostile opposition can reproduce earlier peoples' punishment, adding causal texture to criminal liability.
Little gratitude despite endowed faculties is only a distant lexical parallel to "little" and does not explain 77:46's enjoyment.
Hell is identified as what the mujrimun denied, closely connecting their label with the punishment context of 77:46.
The yellow-camel-like sparks continue the fire image but add little to the command, duration, or guilt in 77:46.
Animals made available for riding and eating portray provision as a gift; this is a broad counterpoint, not a verdict on temporary enjoyment.
Eating and grazing are signs for people of understanding, a remote positive parallel to the imperative in 77:46.
Desired fruits belong to the protected, contrasting the guilty address with the enjoyment of the God-conscious.
Little remembrance concerns following revelation, with only indirect relevance to the culpability of 77:46.
Death after earthly life supplies the mortality horizon that makes enjoyment "a little," without a direct lexical link.
The cry's destruction of wrongdoers offers only a general punishment parallel.
Enjoy your disbelief a little followed by being among the companions of the Fire is a very close imperative-and-consequence parallel.
The verse's inquiry about mujrimun treats criminality as an accountable class, supporting the label in 77:46.
The woe refrain marks the same sequence of warning but adds no new semantic element.
The small number of later people concerns a ranked group, not temporary enjoyment or criminality.
Eating wholesome things is tied to righteous work, a moral counterpoint to the guilty who are told to eat in 77:46.
Giving a little then stopping has no substantive relation beyond the word "little."
At resurrection people suppose they remained only a little, supporting the retrospective compression of present duration.
The declaration that they will taste painful punishment provides the consequence, but not the verse's enjoyment motif.
Their inability to speak continues the judgment scene around the warning to the guilty.
The qualified scarcity of belief is a different use of "little" and does not materially explain 77:46.
Conflicting speech has no close link to enjoyment, duration, or the guilty addressees.
The God-conscious are in shades and springs, a scene-level contrary counterpart to the guilty persons' fate.
Stored food and a small preserved portion model constrained consumption under coming hardship, only indirectly related to temporary enjoyment.
Little sleep as devotional discipline is a different temporal use with minimal bearing on 77:46.
No permission to offer excuses emphasizes the finality of the judgment addressing the guilty.
Enjoyment after rejecting a granted rescue is deferred until later knowledge, closely paralleling culpable enjoyment and its coming disclosure.
Calling them the astray deniers supplies the same audience category as the criminal deniers, without the enjoyment clause.
The earth as a containing place is part of the surah's argument but does not clarify 77:46 directly.
Little belief follows hardened hearts, a distant guilt-related use of "little."
Little laughter and much weeping as recompense supplies a sharp temporal reversal for culpable present pleasure.
The woe against deniers strengthens the broader warning frame but has no direct consumption or brevity link.
Calling a group few is rhetorical minimization, not a contribution to brief enjoyment or criminality.
The humiliating confirmation of resurrection supports the future accountability assumed by 77:46.
The recurring woe continues the denunciation of deniers in the immediate sequence.
Selling signs for a small price gives a morally negative exchange, but only a remote link to the verse's enjoyment.
The night departure while pursued offers a narrative movement toward judgment, with little direct bearing on 77:46.
Refusal to bow identifies concrete defiance within the same woe sequence, helping specify why the addressees are guilty.
Little human knowledge is conceptually unrelated to temporary enjoyment and criminality.
A small exception to night vigil does not clarify the evaluative "little" of 77:46.
The address to the wrapped one adds no discernible connection to 77:46.
Few comply when fighting is prescribed; it is a distant pattern of tested commitment, not enjoyment or penal reprieve.
Restricting present eating to preserve supplies for scarcity is a practical contrast to heedless short-term enjoyment.
The Day of Decision gathers all peoples, providing the adjudicative setting for the warning in 77:46.
The danger of slight inclination is only a lexical "little" parallel and does not illuminate guilty enjoyment.
Eating good provision with gratitude supplies a normative contrast to the guilty addressees' impermanent enjoyment.
The secure resting place in the creation argument has no close link to 77:46.
The prohibition on consuming multiplied usury gives a negative ethical sense of eating, but remains a secondary parallel.
Unaccepted spending from the defiantly disobedient concerns culpability but not enjoyment or its brevity.
Scattered dust is a judgment image with little specific connection to the verse.
Provision and graceful release concern a household choice, only distantly echoing enjoyment as temporary allowance.
Concealing revelation for small gain is described as eating fire, supplying a morally inverted consumption image.
The challenge to deploy their scheme intensifies the immediate judgment confrontation around 77:46.
Travel provision and eventual gathering offer a loose time-bounded sustenance parallel.
The command to send ahead for oneself and meet God is broad accountability language, not a close reading of 77:46.
The lowly fluid creation argument is too remote from the warning about eating and brief enjoyment.
A short interval before regret makes "little" a time until culpability becomes unmistakable, a close temporal parallel.
Their return to themselves and admission of wrongdoing illustrates recognition of blame, but not temporary enjoyment.
Provision for people and livestock is explicitly temporary beside the following great event, a strong granted-sustenance counterpoint.
The commanded night journey while pursued is a narrative judgment parallel with little direct relation to 77:46.
Permitted feeding of the sign-animal is bounded by a prohibition and punishment, contrasting lawful provision with transgression.
The statement that they would fight only little concerns fear in conflict, not 77:46's kind of brevity.
Eating without divine naming is declared defiance, offering a morally accountable consumption parallel.
Little remembrance after relief is a distant gratitude parallel, not an explanation of brief enjoyment.
The tree produces oil and seasoning for eaters, presenting nourishment as provision without the warning or temporal element.
A small exception amid covenant breach has no material link to 77:46.
Abundant eating is bounded by one prohibition whose crossing yields wrongdoing, a basic provision-and-transgression parallel.
It explicitly joins brief worldly enjoyment with return and severe punishment, closely matching 77:46's temporary allowance and culpable horizon.
Those seeking the worldly life and its adornment receive their works there in full, a direct parallel to finite present recompense.
The sequel denies such seekers any hereafter share but Fire, supplying the outcome that qualifies worldly attainment.
It states that worldly life is only a brief enjoyment beside the hereafter, directly explaining the scale of qalilan.
Desire for the immediate is met for a limited recipient before Hell is assigned, a close but differently framed counterpart.
The parable of flourishing growth becoming dry debris clarifies the transience of worldly enjoyment.
Wealth and children are worldly adornment while enduring good deeds are better, supplying a comparative measure for enjoyment.
Worldly splendor is expressly described as enjoyment given to test, preserving its reality while withholding approval or permanence.
The testing of people by good and evil, followed by return, supplies the accountability frame for an interval of enjoyment.
The possibility of a trial and enjoyment for a time directly frames respite as provisional rather than acquittal.
It questions whether wealth and children are mistakenly read as an acceleration of good, challenging favorable readings of present abundance.
The continuation denies that their present provision is recognized correctly, completing the contrary reading of enjoyment as proof of favor.
Extended enjoyment of people and their forebears ends in forgetting the reminder and destruction, closely paralleling indulgence that obscures the end.
Even many years of granted enjoyment do not establish security when the announced consequence arrives.
The arrival of the promised warning completes the temporal reversal of prolonged enjoyment.
It asks what their prior enjoyment then avails, directly denying its ultimate value.
Destroyed settlements that exulted in their livelihood offer a narrative warning against reading prosperity as safety.
What is given in worldly life is enjoyment and adornment, while what remains with God is better and more lasting.
Worldly life is characterized as diversion and play, while the hereafter is the real life, strengthening the evaluative contrast behind 77:46.
Knowing the outward aspect of worldly life while heedless of the hereafter explains how present enjoyment can displace final awareness.
It warns against worldly-life deception and deception about God, giving a general caution against false security in present benefit.
Wealth and children are denied any automatic nearness to God, countering an inference from enjoyed goods to approval.
The warning not to let worldly life deceive directly supports reading the imperative in 77:46 as warning, not endorsement.
Enjoyment is explicitly limited to a time, a concise temporal parallel to qalilan.
A command to let them enjoy for a time presents enjoyment as a bounded deferment rather than final safety.
It expressly calls worldly life a brief enjoyment and the hereafter the abiding home, one of the closest omitted parallels.
What is given is worldly-life enjoyment, while what is with God is better and more enduring for believers.
Worldly ornaments are called enjoyment of worldly life, whereas the hereafter is reserved for the God-conscious.
Taking God's signs in mockery and being deceived by worldly life supplies the denial-and-deception pattern surrounding 77:46.
Those who exhausted their good things and enjoyed them in worldly life are confronted with humiliating punishment, directly joining enjoyment and guilt.
Disbelievers enjoy themselves and eat as cattle eat, while the Fire is their lodging; this is an exceptionally close contrary consumption parallel.
Worldly life is play and diversion, and its rewards are linked to faith and reverence rather than mere consumption.
Leaving them until the day that overwhelms them provides the same deferred-judgment logic as a temporary allowance.
Wealth and children must not distract from remembrance; it supplies a discipline against the diversion latent in enjoyment.
Wealth and children are a trial, supporting a non-approbative reading of enjoyed provision.
People are told to eat of God's provision while the resurrection remains the destination, pairing sustenance with accountability.
Those who deny the discourse are left to a gradual, unrecognized drawing-on, a strong analogue for penal reprieve.
They are left in vain discourse and play until they meet their promised day, a close deferment-before-encounter parallel.
Love of the immediate and neglect of a weighty day directly explains how present preference conflicts with the coming judgment.
At sight of the Hour, prior duration appears no more than an evening or its morning, closely reinforcing the verse's "little."
Preference for the worldly life states the competing attachment that makes temporary enjoyment morally decisive.
The hereafter is better and more enduring, supplying the explicit alternative measure to transient enjoyment.
Rivalry in accumulation distracts, exposing a social form of the preoccupation that can accompany enjoyment.
That distraction lasts until the graves, supplying mortality as the limit that interrupts accumulated enjoyment.
Choosing worldly life over the hereafter results in punishment that is neither lightened nor escaped, directly rejecting a lasting value for present gain.
Worldly life is made attractive to disbelievers, furnishing a contrary account of why enjoyed life can be misread as favor.
Desire for worldly attractions is named and then contrasted with the better return with God, framing enjoyment within an evaluative alternative.
Worldly life is called the enjoyment of delusion, an explicit warning against taking present pleasure as its own verdict.
Selling worldly life for the hereafter supplies the same competing-value frame, though not a consumption image.
The goods of worldly life are contrasted with more abundant gains with God, weakening a short-term acquisition logic.
Worldly life is only play and diversion, while the hereafter is better for the reverent, a close evaluative counterpart.
Those deceived by worldly life are left with their diversion and play before a severe consequence, extending the warning pattern.
Taking religion as play and being deceived by worldly life joins diversion, forgetfulness, and the day of recompense.
Wealth and children are not signs to admire but means of worldly distress and a final death in disbelief, countering prosperity-as-approval.
Enjoying one's allotted share like prior peoples is followed by blame, a direct historical parallel to transient indulgence.
The worldly-life parable moves from attractive growth to destruction, clarifying how visible flourishing can rapidly lose its standing.
Loving worldly life over the hereafter and turning from God's path supplies a direct causal account of misplaced preference.
Good in this world is affirmed while the hereafter remains better, preserving a secondary, non-denying contrast to 77:46.
Worldly and hereafter gifts are both extended by God, but this granting is not presented as an unrestricted endorsement.
Earthly adornment is made a test of who acts best, placing attractive provision under trial rather than final valuation.
The desire for worldly adornment is set against remaining with those who remember God, describing a practical resistance to diversion.
The present worldly life is explicitly limited in contrast to a chosen final commitment, reinforcing the bounded temporal frame.
One may take a share of the world but must seek the final abode, a balanced contrary reading to unbounded present enjoyment.
Worldly-life affection becomes mutual repudiation on the Day of Resurrection, exposing a present social attachment's future reversal.
Prosperity is voiced as a reason for disbelief, showing how abundance can become a ground of culpable confidence.
The patient are rewarded without measure, contrasting the narrowness of temporary worldly calculation.
Those seeking the harvest of worldly life receive some of it but have no share in the hereafter, directly limiting worldly pursuit.
The claim that only worldly life exists names the outlook that 77:46's judgment context overturns.
Turning from remembrance while desiring only worldly life gives an explicit attentional mechanism for temporary enjoyment's dominance.
The narrative of abundant wealth granted with ease but followed by demand and punishment offers a personal case of provision without approval.
Intense love of wealth gives a concise dispositional parallel to the attachment that distorts enjoyment.
